options.misconception: Reported joules instead of converting to kilojoules
Divided mass by latent heat instead of multiplying
Correct application of the principle
Used a factor of one hundred rather than one thousand

questions.explanation: During a phase change the temperature stays constant while energy goes into rearranging the structure, so Q equals mass times specific latent heat. Here 14 g times 401 J per g gives 5614 J, or 5.61 kJ after dividing by one thousand.
questions.hint: Q = m L, then convert joules to kilojoules.

Left the answer in joules instead of kilojoules
Correct application of the principle

questions.explanation: When heat capacity is given per mole, the heat required is Q equals n times Cm times delta T. Multiplying 0.5 mol by 72 J per mol K by 60 K and dividing by one thousand yields 2.16 kJ.

questions.stem: Trial 471788305: an ideal gas of helium with 2.5 mol expands isothermally at 431 K from 1.4 L to 4.6 L; how much heat must be supplied, in kJ?

options.misconception: Halved the temperature in the nRT factor
Correct application of the principle
Omitted the logarithm from the work expression
Altered the volume ratio by adding one to it

questions.explanation: For an ideal gas at constant temperature the internal energy does not change, so by the first law the heat supplied equals the work done by the gas, nRT ln(Vf over Vi). With the given volumes and temperature this is 10.70 kJ; heat must flow in to balance the expansion work.
questions.hint: At constant T for an ideal gas, Q = W = nRT ln(Vf/Vi).

questions.stem: Trial 465579706: starting at 343 K, an ideal gas of carbon dioxide with gamma 1.4 expands adiabatically from 2.8 L to 8.1 L; find the final temperature.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Used gamma rather than gamma minus one as the exponent
Inverted the initial-to-final volume ratio
Assumed temperature scales linearly with volume

questions.explanation: For a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas process T V raised to gamma minus one is constant, so Tf equals Ti times (Vi over Vf) to the power gamma minus one. With gamma 1.4 the exponent is 0.4, giving a final temperature of 224.0 K; expansion cools the gas because it does work with no heat entering.
questions.hint: Use Tf = Ti (Vi/Vf)^(gamma - 1) for adiabatic expansion.

questions.explanation: Because the device returns to its starting state each cycle, the change in internal energy over a full cycle is zero, so the net work output equals the net heat input Qh minus Qc. That gives 320 J per cycle; the rejected heat is not available as work.
